TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
TUESDAY, 07 JULY 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 3, DAY 7
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC, COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH MATT SHERMAN AND
CHRISTOPHER BESHARA, COUNSEL ASSISTING

<THE HEARING COMMENCED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Lancaster.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you, Commissioner. This morning's two witnesses
are called on behalf of TikTok Australia which has representatives at the bar table.
MS MIRZABEGIAN SC: Commissioner, my name is Mirzabegian, and I appear
with Mr Rogers for TikTok Australia.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you, that is noted.
MR LANCASTER SC: I call Mr Zachary Hecht.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
<ZACHARY HECHT, SWORN
COMMISSIONER: Yes, thank you, sir. Do take a seat.
MR HECHT: Thank you.
MR LANCASTER SC: Mr Hecht, please state your full name.
MR HECHT: Zachary Hecht.
MR LANCASTER SC: Your address is known to the Commission. You are the
Global Head of Policy, Trust and Safety for TikTok?
MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have provided two statements in writing to the
Commission on behalf of TikTok Australia Proprietary Limited. The first of those
statements is dated 28 May 2026. Are the contents of that statement true and correct?
MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, that statement bears the ID
STAT.8999.0071.0002, and I tender that statement.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. That statement will be admitted as an exhibit.
MR LANCASTER SC: Mr Hecht, you've prepared a shorter, more recent statement
of 4 July 2026. Are the contents of that statement true and correct?
MR HECHT: Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, I tender that statement. It bears the ID
STAT.8999.0001.0448.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. That will also be received as an exhibit.
MR LANCASTER SC: Mr Hecht, as I mentioned, you are the Global Head of
Policy, Trust and Safety for TikTok?
MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You first commenced in that role in December 2025?
MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Before that, you held a number of policy roles in Trust and
Safety at TikTok?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in your role, you lead global policy development for
TikTok on issues such as hate speech and antisemitism?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you lead the teams that are responsible for ensuring
that TikTok safety policies are fit for purpose and that enforcement occurs in
accordance with those policies; is that right?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: You are based in New York?
MR HECHT: I am.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have travelled to Australia in order to give evidence
voluntarily to assist the Commission?
MR HECHT: I have.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, TikTok is a global entertainment platform launched
in 2017?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: It was originally launched and operated by a company
called ByteDance?

MR HECHT: I believe so, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: In January this year, TikTok's US operations were
transferred from ByteDance to a new entity known as TikTok USDS Joint Venture
LLC; is that right?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: As a result of that or transactions connected with that
change, ByteDance retains a 19.9 per cent interest in TikTok USDS Joint Venture
LLC?
MR HECHT: I'm not sure on the percentage, but it sounds right to me.
MR LANCASTER SC: Just to address the corporate structure in Australia, TikTok
Australia Proprietary Limited is incorporated in Australia?
MR HECHT: I believe so.
MR LANCASTER SC: The Australian entity does not provide the TikTok platform
in Australia?
MR HECHT: It does not.
MR LANCASTER SC: The platform is provided and operated in Australia by an
entity known as TikTok Pte, which is a Singaporean entity; is that right?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is the Singaporean entity owned and controlled by
ByteDance or by the US joint venture or by some other entity?
MR HECHT: Corporate governance isn't the area that I focus on, but I believe it's
controlled by ByteDance.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. And are TikTok's systems and content the same
globally whether provided by the US joint venture or the Singaporean entity or do
they vary?
MR HECHT: Would you mind repeating the question.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes. Do TikTok's systems and content - are they consistent
globally whether they're provided by the US joint venture or by the Singaporean
entity?

MR HECHT: There are similarities and global operations oversee the platform, but
there are differentiations that take place. Corporate governance isn't the area that I'm
most expert in, in my role, but there are similarities.
MR LANCASTER SC: When it comes to the application of Trust and Safety
provisions, is there a global uniformity in the way they are applied to TikTok
content?
MR HECHT: Yes, although there could be differentiations in certain entities like
the US joint venture.
MR LANCASTER SC: I see. Outside the US, the rest of the world is treated
consistently so far as Trust and Safety controls and content moderation and the like.
MR HECHT: That is the general approach.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, TikTok Australia received a notice from the
Commission calling for statements from the production of documents?
MR HECHT: I believe so, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in response to that notice, other companies in the
TikTok group, that is, other than just TikTok Australia, have voluntarily produced
a large number of documents to the Commission, including internal records such as
emails and papers.
MR HECHT: I wasn't involved in the document production but I do believe so, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you and Mr Richey have, as I indicated, voluntarily
provided statements to the Commission.
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, can I ask you about the services offered by TikTok
and focusing for the moment on iOS and Android users, TikTok offers a short-form
video service that presents users with short videos?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: As a user scrolls through their device, they're shown short
videos produced by content creators.
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Using a tab at the top of the mobile device screen, the user
can view videos created by those who they are following.

MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: If the user selects a For You tab, they are shown a curated
selection of videos selected by an algorithm or a recommender system.
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: The iOS and Android services also provide a Community
tab which displays photo and video content in a manner that's broadly similar to
Instagram's grid configuration.
MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: In the case of each of the functions described as Following,
For You and Community, users are generally able to like, comment on, bookmark
and share the relevant item of content?
MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: The app also contains a Live option where users are able to
stream content live and those watching the content are able to participate in a chat
that's superimposed at the bottom of the live feed. Is that right?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, there's also a dedicated STEM, S-T-E-M, feed that
contains content relevant to science, technology, engineering and mathematics.
MR HECHT: I believe so, at least in some markets yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: In the Australian market?
MR HECHT: I believe so, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: There is also an aspect of the app known as the TikTok
Shop, which is an e-commerce layer that lets creators and sellers sell through
shoppable videos, as they're called?
MR HECHT: In some markets, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Does that apply in Australia?
MR HECHT: I'm not sure at the moment. I believe not yet, but I'm not sure on that.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, the app also contains an inbox; is that a generally
available function?

MR HECHT: It is.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that allows users to send messages to other users of
TikTok?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, TikTok also has a web page that may be accessed
through an internet browser that replicates much of the functionality of TikTok as it
appears on mobile services.
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is it fair to say that the very great majority of TikTok users
access the service through either the iOS or Android mobile devices' services?
MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in your role, you are responsible for developing and
implementing content-related policies that cover the range of services delivered
through the TikTok app and web page; is that right?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, can I ask you about the policy framework that
TikTok applies. TikTok has terms of service?
MR HECHT: We do.
MR LANCASTER SC: The terms of service make clear that access to, and use of,
the services provided by TikTok is subject to your Community Guidelines?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And the Community Guidelines apply in the same terms
globally; is that right?
MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And the current set of guidelines took effect on 13
September 2025?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Within those guidelines are the Safety and Civility
Guidelines?

MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And they also apply to content that is displayed to
Australian end-users?
MR HECHT: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, the Community Guidelines themselves address
content moderation and the steps taken to moderate content, don't they?
MR HECHT: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: So, just in brief summary, the approach taken by TikTok is,
firstly, the removal of content that falls under what are described as the "Not
Allowed" rules?
MR HECHT: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that is a process that happens automatically by the
application of a system process; is that right?
MR HECHT: We take a number of approaches to moderate content. We moderate
all content that's posted on the platform, and we also would then moderate
subsequently but, yes, we do moderate all content based on those guidelines.
MR LANCASTER SC: I will come back to that in a moment. A second aspect of
moderation is that there's certain age restrictions - well, there's certain content to
which age restrictions are applied that prevent it being posted to users of particular
ages?
MR HECHT: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thirdly, there are what's called For You Feed Standards
that govern the types of content that are eligible to be recommended in the For You
feed.
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: I'll come back to the recommender algorithm a little later.
And, fourthly, the fourth aspect of content moderation is that it provides users with
some tools and resources to manage their own experience of TikTok by changing
their content settings; is that right?
MR HECHT: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And what can a user do in that regard to control the content
that they receive?

MR HECHT: The main way that users are recommended content is through their
own engagement and behaviour on the platform, but then in addition to that, we give
users a number of options. Some of those would include the use of a keyword
feature, which would enable them to filter any content out of their feed that contains
that word or that theme. In addition, users have the ability to block or unfollow
certain users. They have the ability to click "not interested" buttons. And that's on top
of the natural curation that happens to curate their own feed more.
MR LANCASTER SC: So in that context, a user could enter one or more particular
terms to prevent content containing those words appearing on their feed; is that
right?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Are there - can there - I withdraw that. Is there any facility
in TikTok by which users concerned not to receive content of a particular type are
provided with a template or an example of the kind of things they could put into that
content-controlling page to prevent them seeing what they regard as objectionable
material?
MR HECHT: I don't believe so. There is a feature for a "managed topics" which is
rolled out in certain markets and has been tested where users could toggle up certain
themes, but otherwise, I'm not aware of any template.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, TikTok maintains Hate Speech and Hateful
Behaviour Guidelines.
MR HECHT: We do.
MR LANCASTER SC: Which fall within the Community Guidelines?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, can I bring up a copy of the guidelines. It's
RCD.5999.0001.0030. If we focus on the text at the foot of this page, please, if we
can make that legible, under the heading Hate Speech and Hateful Behaviour. The
document indicates:
"We don't allow hate speech, hateful behaviour or promotion of hateful ideologies."
This - and I'll just ask you a question about that in a moment. I will just show you the
next page of the policy. If the top part of that page can be -the top half of that page
can be zoomed. Thank you. "Hateful ideologies", "protected groups" and "protected
attributes" are all given some definition in that context, and you have referred in your
first statement at paragraph 45 to the guidelines prohibiting antisemitism and other

forms of hate speech and identify race and religion as protected attributes. Can I just
ask you some specific questions about the page.
The first is, there's a section defining hateful ideologies as:
"Systems of beliefs that exclude, oppress or otherwise discriminate against
individuals based on their protected attributes."
Hateful ideologies in the way that TikTok understands and applies the term in the
context of this policy includes antisemitism; is that right?
MR HECHT: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Then under the definition of "protected groups", refers to:
"Individuals or communities that share protected attributes."
"Protected attributes" is then defined by the list that appears below it. And is it right
that anyone or other of those attributes, if the basis for the discrimination referred to
in the definition of hateful ideologies occurs, would be content that TikTok would
regard as contrary or violating its guidelines?
MR HECHT: Yes, we would remove content that discriminates on the basis of
those attributes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, you may not be in a position to agree with this, but
the list of protected attributes is longer and more specific than a number of other
social media platforms that we've seen in their identification of protected
characteristics. Is that your understanding?
MR HECHT: I'm focused on the TikTok platform, and I'm not sure of what the list
of other platforms would be in this moment, but what I can say is this list is informed
by global human rights standards, as is noted here, and is what we believe
individuals should be protected from discrimination against.
MR LANCASTER SC: And was the - you've referred in your statement, I think,
to - or perhaps you haven't referred to it, but TikTok has a Safety and Content
Advisory Council?
MR HECHT: We do.
MR LANCASTER SC: And could you explain the function of that council?
MR HECHT: Certainly. That's a council that we will consult with to inform the
development of our policies to hear from different impacted communities, but also to
hear from people that are experts in their particular field. We have Safety Advisory
Councils around the world. I know my colleague Valient Richey will be speaking to

the Commission and he's the individual that oversees that, but it's a process that I'm
also very familiar with.
MR LANCASTER SC: Does TikTok draw on Australian members or experts in the
context of its advisory council work?
MR HECHT: I believe so, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you mentioned the recognition and inclusion of global
human rights standards in creating this list of protected attributes. Was that based on
advice or consultation with the advisory council?
MR HECHT: I'm not positive it was specific to the advisory council, although we
will have certainly discussed it. But we also consult with a number of experts in
different fields and it will be informed by that, as well as conversations with
impacted communities.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, is it right that there is then an application in the
content moderation framework that TikTok uses, a traffic light scheme, as it were,
that identifies things that are not allowed, things that might render content ineligible
for particular feed users or age users and, thirdly, things that are allowed?
MR HECHT: We don't refer to it as a traffic light system but, yes, we have
moderation teams or automated systems applying policies that will result in one of
those outcomes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Could I take you further down the page, that's on the
screen, if you can zoom back out and look at the bottom half of the page, please.
Under the Not Allowed heading, is it right to understand these as a non-exhaustive
list of examples of the policy's application for content that is not allowed on the
platform?
MR HECHT: That's correct. This is our attempt to illustrate what we prohibit, but it
is not an exhaustive list of what's not allowed on the platform, but to provide that
overview.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, you referred earlier to content that is put forward by
a content creator to be posted or lodged on the system as going through a process of
content moderation at that point; is that right?
MR HECHT: Every piece of content that's uploaded is moderated at that point
proactively.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that automated system of moderation - it is automated;
is that right?

MR HECHT: We have automated moderation and we also have human moderation.
At the point of upload, auto-moderation oversees everything.
MR LANCASTER SC: At the point of a user or a content creator first attempting to
load something, it would be the automated system that looks at it first?
MR HECHT: Correct. And in certain instances, the automated system can then
route it for further review if it needs further guidance or input.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is that referral, then, to a human reviewer?
MR HECHT: In those instances, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And does that occur when the automated system sees
something that it analyses as a line-ball decision as to whether it ought to be allowed
or not?
MR HECHT: The automated systems will take action when there's a high
confidence level that something is violative, then there's a lower level of confidence
where something might need further review, and it could be routed for human
review. And in certain instances, there's no understanding that content is violative at
that point, and then it would be available on the platform.
MR LANCASTER SC: And is the automated system trained or required to apply,
for example, this list of bullet points of what is not allowed on the system?
MR HECHT: This list of bullet points, as well as additional guidelines that further
illustrate this for our teams that are either developing those models or also tagging
content.
MR LANCASTER SC: This type of list is updated from time to time?
MR HECHT: Correct. We update our Community Guidelines at this point once
yearly, and it's something that we are looking to continue doing. And this, as you
noted, was updated last in September of 2025.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that's something that your team undertakes, the
process of review and updating if necessary.
MR HECHT: Yes, I myself and my team oversee the Community Guidelines as
well as the updates to those.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, you see the second bullet point on the page:
"Supporting or spreading hateful ideologies..."
One of the sub-bullet points is:

"Claims of supremacy over a protected group, such as white supremacy, misogyny,
anti-LGBTQ+ hate, antisemitism or Islamophobia."
Is that right?
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Other conduct is - identified as hateful ideologies is the
second sub-bullet point:
"Hateful conspiracies targeting a protected group, such as the 'Great Replacement
Theory' or claims that Jewish people control the media."
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And then the next main bullet point on the page is:
"Denying or minimising well-documented historical atrocities against protected
groups, such as the Holocaust or the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda."
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And further down again:
"Blaming an entire group for actions committed by one person within that group."
What sort of examples does that cover?
MR HECHT: So, yes, that's there, and it could be, for instance, if a Jewish
individual had committed a crime and then an individual that was posting or sharing
content blamed all of the Jewish people for that crime, and so we would prohibit that.
MR LANCASTER SC: Was this list of content that's not allowed developed in
consultation with any expert advice or consultants from members of the Australian
Jewish community or, more broadly, the global Jewish community?
MR HECHT: This list reflects our internal policy approach, and I don't believe that
the specific publication that you see here was informed by those conversations.
However, the policies that this public document is based on are certainly informed by
conversations with members of the Jewish community, as well as experts in the field
of hate speech.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, as you no doubt appreciated, one of the questions that
the Commission is concerned to inquire into and that your statement addresses is the
threshold for removal of antisemitic content from TikTok?

MR HECHT: I understand that, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, you have said in the statement quite clearly that:
"Content that is identified as being antisemitic will be content that is in violation of
the Safety and Civility Guidelines."
And:
"It is removed from TikTok."
MR HECHT: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: You are referring there to, in a summary form, to your
understanding of the operation both of the automated system for review of content
and also the approach that the reviewers and moderators take; is that right?
MR HECHT: Correct. The Community Guidelines are agnostic to the approach of
moderation. They are what we apply for all forms of moderation.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, one aspect of the policy that I'd ask you to explain is
the section dealing with the For You feed and the steps taken against those who
violate the guidelines. So when a content creator posts content that is identified and
is removed from the system, either by an automated process or by a reviewer, what
happens with the content creator and their account?
MR HECHT: When we remove content, it's no longer available on the platform,
and as we articulate in the Account section of our Community Guidelines, we may
ban an account when there are multiple violations. In addition, when there are
absolutely egregious violations, we ban a user after a single instance. It's not
necessarily covered by the Hate Speech and Hateful Ideology section but we also
prohibit incitement to violence. And so when there's an act of incitement to violence,
which may be against the Jewish people and would therefore be antisemitic, an
account would be banned right away.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is there a particular number of violations that need to occur
before TikTok will remove a content creator's access to TikTok?
MR HECHT: It's a dynamic system that looks at violations over the amount of
content posted, as well as over a specific time period. And so that would be
something that would be adjusted over to time to ensure that we are effectively
taking bad actors off of our platform.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is there a suspension and then a removal process? Or is it
the case that, according to the application of that dynamic standard, once a content
creator has been identified as sufficiently problematic, they're simply removed from
access to the service?

MR HECHT: As of now, it is almost always directly removed. There are certain
features like Live where a user that violates once may also be suspended and not
have access to that feature, and we are regularly trying to identify the best way to
ensure that bad actors are not engaging on the platform but also educate users so they
might know that they have to change their behaviour to remain on the platform.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, can I take you to the Enforcement section of the
guidelines. This is a document RCD.5999.0001.0027. And in the top half of the
page, the reference to Public Interest Exceptions. Now, just for context in your
statement in paragraph 50, you observe that:
"TikTok distinguishes between content that promotes antisemitism and content that
includes or refers to hateful material for the purposes such as education,
documentary reporting, counter-speech, condemnation, or satire."
MR HECHT: That's correct, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: In that context, what do you mean by "counter-speech"?
MR HECHT: What we mean is an individual would be condemning a harmful or
a hateful act, so in the instance of the conversation today, it would be that perhaps
somebody might have said something antisemitic, a user might upload a video of that
and then they might actively condemn that. I think one of the things that's important
about our approach, which is also articulated here on this page, is we err on the side
of caution and safety. So if somebody simply uploads an image and they make
a comment that we can't tell either way, we are going to still remove that. We need
active condemnation; we need active behaviour from the user so we can tell the
intent and we can tell that they're doing it in order to condemn.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have also said in paragraph 50 that:
"TikTok ... permits discussion of social issues affecting protected groups, including
policy debates, provided the content does not attack individuals or groups on the
basis of a protected attribute."
MR HECHT: That's accurate, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, in that context, is there a residual area of discretion
for TikTok to permit content that would otherwise violate the guidelines according to
this assessment of whether or not it's part of a policy debate?
MR HECHT: No. If something is a part of a policy debate but still contravenes our
prohibition on hate speech, we would remove it. This is noted in the document to just
convey that we do recognise that sometimes a protected group might be criticised in
a way that is not hateful, and we might enable that as long as it doesn't start to
characterise an entire protected group in a specific way or dehumanise them.

MR LANCASTER SC: And as you understand it, the - or as you describe it,
comments posted in response to an uploaded video might amount to a discussion of
social issues or a policy debate in some circumstances; is that right?
MR HECHT: In some circumstances, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Does that occur very often, according to your
understanding of the platform?
MR HECHT: Would you mind clarifying this for me, please?
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes. How often would comments made by users on an
uploaded TikTok video amount to a policy debate?
MR HECHT: I don't have an estimate of how often that occurs, but I would note
that the initial video would have to be within the allowance of our Community
Guidelines, so if the initial video is a violation, it's coming off the platform and is not
available to comment on. It could be that a user uploads a piece of content about an
ongoing social issue and then users might comment, but those comments would also
have to be within the bounds of our Community Guidelines. If they're hateful, they're
being removed. It doesn't matter if the larger context is a policy or a public debate.
MR LANCASTER SC: I see. Thank you. Now, there's a Detection in Reporting
section of the policy. I'm not sure we need to go to it, but it indicates that TikTok
does aim to, as you've said, to remove content or accounts that violate its rules before
they're viewed or shared through that automated review process, or that it might be
flagged and then go to a moderator.
MR HECHT: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, the process that occurs when the automated system
refers it to a human reviewer or a human moderator are there timeframes that are
applied to that? In other words, is there a required standard of the reviewer or the
moderator to deal with those matters within a certain period?
MR HECHT: It's a dynamic system. We strive to review content immediately. If
content is violative and clearly violative, the automated system would remove it right
away. In other instances, it might not be available until a human moderator reviews
it, and so it's a dynamic system that depends on the amount of content that's being
uploaded, as well as a number of the attributes of the content itself.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in the instances where the automated system does refer
newly uploaded content to a moderator or a reviewer, is that content visible until it's
dealt with by the moderator? Or is it not allowed to be uploaded until it is given the
tick, as it were?

MR HECHT: I am not the expert on the system and the dynamic nature of it, but my
understanding is that it would depend. In certain instances, if the content is related to
a specific area of harm, it wouldn't be permitted on the platform. However, in other
instances, it's might be permitted on the platform until it's reviewed. But I know that
our system is designed to err on the side of caution for content that might be harmful
or violative.
MR LANCASTER SC: And then when - there's also a facility for other users to
report or complain about content that's posted?
MR HECHT: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is there a timeframe within which TikTok requires its
moderators or reviewers to address those complaints?
MR HECHT: My understanding is it's also a dynamic system. We strive to review
reports and complaints as soon as possible, although in some instances, based on the
amount of content, it could take a differential amount of time.
MR LANCASTER SC: All right. There's no objective or intention to deal with it
within, say, 24 hours or 48 hours of which you are aware?
MR HECHT: Not that I am personally aware of, but what I do want to also point
out is every piece of content on the platform has been reviewed at the point of
upload. So there's not an instance where a piece of content would have been reported
where it hasn't been reviewed. This is an additional layer of review that would be
taking place on the receipt of a report. I would also just note that when users report
content, we also provide them with an update. So if you report content, you receive
information in your inbox about when that report was reviewed and the outcome of
that report.
MR LANCASTER SC: In terms of the particular tools that are used by the
